dailyRead: Start with the thing that actually moved, because it is not a central bank. The war premium in crude is no longer bleeding out slowly - it is being unwound, and fast. WTI is 84.87 and down 1.00% today, Brent 91.72 and down 0.78%, and those small daily numbers sit on top of a 3.2% to 3.5% collapse on Monday that took the monthly moves to minus 13.88% and minus 16.27%. A day ago this file had WTI at 87.68 with the month at minus 9.92%. The cause is specific and it is the first genuinely new fact on this board in a week: transits through the Strait of Hormuz are recovering. United Against Nuclear Iran puts US-facilitated transits at an average 33.8 vessels a day with a record 135 over the November 8 to 11 window, and the Joint Maritime Information Centre counted 83 from November 12 to 14, about 28 a day. Set alongside the International Energy Agency's forecast of a fourth-quarter surplus and Goldman Sachs' call for Brent to average 88 dollars in 2027 and ease to 78 by that year's end, and the premium has a reason to leave rather than merely an absence of reasons to stay. One correction of emphasis is owed, though, because a wire framing has gone too far: some reporting has Hormuz flows back near pre-war levels and that is not what the counts show. The IMF's PortWatch recorded three transits on November 8 against a pre-crisis baseline near 85 a day, the JMIC baseline is about 138 a day for 2025, and the JMIC still rates the strait severe with deliberate hostile action highly likely and 183 confirmed regional incidents since March 1. The direction has changed decisively; the level has not. Two more tankers were reported to have exploded in the strait on Monday and the United States struck Iranian missile launchers across southern Iran on Sunday night. So the trade is a falling premium on a still-dangerous waterway, which means the downside is now a slide rather than a bleed while the upside remains a gap. The second consequence is the one that costs money, and it is Canadian. The Bank of Canada hiked in October specifically to stop high energy prices spreading into other goods and services, and energy has now fallen roughly 14% in a month. Stack that on yesterday's October CPI, which missed on two of its three red-folder lines with the m/m at plus 0.2% against plus 0.3%, trimmed at 1.8% against 1.9% and headline y/y stuck at 3.1% where a Reuters poll wanted 3.2%, and on core inflation down to 2.0% from 2.2% so that the two preferred cores now average 1.9% - below the midpoint - against a jobless rate at a six-month high of 6.7% and a third consecutive monthly fall in employment at minus 4,700. The Canadian dollar goes from minus one to minus two, and USD/CAD at 1.42994 becomes the widest score gap on the board at four points. Note what it did not do today: the pair is plus 0.01% and went nowhere, so this is a thesis widening rather than a move to chase. Third, the Reserve Bank of Australia, where a leg of this file's own argument broke and should be said plainly. The November minutes landed at 02:30 and they were hawkish, not dovish. Six of nine members judged the cash rate at 4.85% was not clearly sufficient to return inflation to target, citing rising inflation pressures, strong services inflation and a likely higher neutral rate. The three dissenters did not argue the cycle is finished - they argued it was prudent to wait and assess the 100 basis points already delivered this year, pointing to delayed effects, higher-than-expected unemployment and the housing downturn. Yesterday's file named its invalidation as the minutes showing the dissenters held on substance rather than timing. They held on timing, and the majority leaned the other way, so the Aussie moves from minus two to minus one and every Aussie short on this board loses a notch. Price agreed: AUD/USD is 0.67386 and plus 0.03% after a 0.58% fall, AUD/NZD plus 0.11%, AUD/CAD plus 0.04%. This does not make the Aussie strong - core inflation at 3.6% is the highest on the board but so is the policy rate, September employment was minus 39,329, copper is 5.97 and down 8.61% on the month, and the market still implies roughly an 82% chance rates have peaked while CommBank expects a December hold. It makes the short less safe, and Thursday's October employment at 02:30 against a plus 25,500 forecast is now the two-way risk on a trade that has lost its hawkish-minutes insurance. Fourth, the kiwi, which is the weakest currency on this board today and takes the downgrade the Aussie just escaped. NZD/USD is 0.54947 and minus 0.06%, a sixth consecutive losing session and fresh 18-month lows, and it is weakest against everything: EUR/NZD plus 0.25% through 2.00, GBP/NZD plus 0.26%, AUD/NZD plus 0.11%, NZD/JPY minus 0.24%. The Q4 inflation expectations survey at 04:00 was the red folder and it did not rescue it - two-year expectations edged to 2.36% from 2.34% on TradingEconomics, barely a move, though the one-year gauge jumped to 2.92% from 2.60% and survey respondents put the official cash rate at 3.05% by the end of December, which is a hike. That is the tension worth holding: the rate path still points up, with the committee having said tighter policy is likely to be required and TradingEconomics forecasting 3.00% on December 9 while ANZ expects a pause, but a currency making new lows for six sessions cannot be scored alongside sterling. The kiwi goes from plus one to minus one on the backward evidence with the December 9 statement as the clearest invalidation. Governor Breman spoke at 02:00 and nothing from those remarks is yet verifiable. Fifth, the dollar and the Fed, where the path got more hawkish, not less. CME-based pricing for December 9 is now 95.7% for a quarter-point against 92% to 93.5% yesterday, and the fifty-point tail has actually shrunk to 4.3% from the 6.5% to 8% this file carried - but the hawkishness moved out the curve instead, with January 2027 cumulative pricing at 69.4% for fifty basis points and 27.6% for twenty-five. In other words the market has stopped arguing about December and started pricing a second hike. Waller, who speaks at 16:10, has said a fifty-point move should be considered in December. The 10-year is 5.125%. And yet DXY is 103.472 and minus 0.11%, the third session running in which the dollar has not gained on a risk-off tape, which is the one crack in a plus two worth watching. Retail sales at 15:30 is the test, and note the forecast was cut to plus 0.1% from plus 0.2% with core at plus 0.4%. Sixth, a quieter correction on the metals and on Europe. Gold is 3,875.92 and plus 0.50%, silver 47.61 and plus 1.42%, platinum plus 1.44% - a bounce after silver's one-year low, and a modest one that does not change the axis. The month still reads minus 6.40% for gold and minus 16.60% for silver, the 10-year is above five, and nothing in the Fed pricing has turned. Keep both shorts and treat the bounce as the risk being priced rather than the thesis changing. Europe is the opposite nuance. EU gas is 84.89 euros and now down 3.58% on the month where a day ago it was up 2.39%, which removes the headwind this file has carried against the DAX for weeks and, more importantly, undercuts the argument that the European Central Bank's December hike is being bought with energy. Headline HICP is 4.0% against core at 2.5%; if the energy leg is now falling, the case for anything beyond December 17 weakens even as the market prices three more moves over the coming year against 46 of 71 Reuters economists calling 2.75% the peak. The euro stays at plus one, but the reason has quietly become weaker rather than stronger. Finally sterling, which has done nothing - 1.31974 and plus 0.09% - and remains the only December outside the United States that is not effectively priced, which is the whole reason it sits above the euro. That gets tested twice in thirty hours: the labour market at 09:00 today with average earnings forecast to slow to 3.5% from 3.7%, then October CPI tomorrow at 09:00 forecast 3.6% from 3.5% with core steady at 2.8%, followed by Bailey at 09:30 and again at 17:00. One more event sits outside every red-folder list and can reverse half this board: Nvidia reports after the US close, its first quarter after Jensen Huang's exit, with consensus near 109 billion dollars of revenue, adjusted earnings about 2.47 dollars a share and options pricing a move near 7.8%. The stock is 156.14 and down 4.12% going in. A beat restores risk appetite and hits the yen upgrade, the silver short and the Aussie short at once; a miss does the reverse.

USD.when: December 9 at 21:00, with new projections, and today's retail sales beat removed the nearer downside risk to it
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Fed funds rate at 4.00% for October as the upper bound of the 3.75% to 4.00% range, held on October 28 with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a quarter-point rise. Today's red folder went the hawkish way on both lines: October retail sales plus 0.2% against a plus 0.1% forecast and core plus 0.6% against plus 0.4%, with TradingEconomics confirming both actuals. Both still decelerated sharply from plus 0.8% and plus 0.9% in September, so this is a beat on a bar cut twice rather than an accelerating consumer. Going in, CME-based measures were 95.7% for a quarter-point on December 9, the fifty-point December tail 4.3% and January 2027 cumulative pricing 69.4% for fifty basis points; no post-release reading is verifiable yet. One correction to this file: Waller's fifty-point condition, set out in London on November 10, was core CPI near 0.3% or higher - which October already met - not retail sales, so today adds to the quarter-point case rather than the fifty. He speaks at 16:10 and Hammack at 16:30. Wednesday's October 28 minutes at 21:00 are now the week's real Fed test and will show how wide the hawkish bloc is.

EUR.when: December 17 at 15:15, the final meeting of 2026 and, on the economists' consensus, the final hike of the cycle
EUR.note: The deposit facility rate is 2.50% on TradingEconomics - the main refinancing rate is 2.65% and is not the policy rate for this board - after an October 29 hold. All 71 economists in the Reuters poll taken November 10 to 12 expect 2.75% on December 17; 46 see that as the peak and 25 see another move in early 2027, while the market is the more hawkish side with ECB Watch near 92% for December and traders priced for three more moves over the next year. What changed today cuts against the hawks and it is the energy leg: EU gas is 84.89 euros and now down 3.58% on the month, where a day ago it was up 2.39%. Headline HICP at 4.0% against core steady at 2.5% means this hike is bought with energy, so falling gas weakens the case for anything past December rather than strengthening it. Final October CPI lands Wednesday 12:00 and Lagarde speaks Wednesday 16:25, Thursday 15:30 and Friday 10:15.

GBP.when: December 17 at 14:00, still genuinely live, and tested twice in the next thirty hours
GBP.note: Bank Rate is 4.00% after the November 5 increase, voted 8-1 with Catherine Mann dissenting for a half-point to 4.25% - the first rise since August 2023. The Bank projects CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year from 3.5% before energy effects fade, and said activity data have generally been stronger than expected. Bailey has signalled another increase may be needed unless inflation risks ease while warning against reading November as the start of a long series, and Lombardelli has kept December open without committing. The labour market lands today at 09:00 with average earnings forecast to slow to 3.5% three-month on year from 3.7%, the claimant count at plus 25,400 and unemployment at 4.7%; October CPI follows Wednesday 09:00 forecast 3.6% from 3.5% with core steady at 2.8% and RPI 4.1%, then Bailey at 09:30 and again at 17:00. This is the only December outside the United States that is not effectively priced.

JPY.when: December 18 at 05:00, close to fully priced, with intervention the nearer event risk
JPY.note: The policy rate is 1.25% after an 8-1 October hold, with Hajime Takata dissenting for a faster move toward neutral, following consecutive quarter-point hikes in June and September that took borrowing costs to their highest since April 1995. A contracting quarter did not change it: Q3 GDP was flat at 0.0% quarter on quarter and minus 0.1% annualised, and TradingEconomics still carries 1.50% for December 18, with traders reported as fully pricing the move and Commerzbank explicitly saying the soft GDP does not alter its call. The nearer driver is the Ministry of Finance rather than the Bank: Tokyo has warned against yen selling since USD/JPY reached 160.00 and Finance Minister Katayama said the government would respond appropriately to currency moves, which is holding the pair off the line without a yen being spent - the Ministry used a record 15.4 trillion yen defending it between July 30 and August 3. One honest revision: this file has been attributing the yen's firmness to a carry unwind, and reporting does not support that framing - what is documented is haven demand in the tech selloff plus the verbal cap. National core CPI lands Friday 01:30, forecast 2.3% from 2.1%.

AUD.when: December 8 at 05:30, still the base case, but the minutes have made it a closer call than the market has it
AUD.note: The cash rate is 4.85% on TradingEconomics after the November 3 increase from 4.60%, carried 6-3 - the fifth hike of the year and the highest since late 2008. The November minutes at 02:30 were the hawkish surprise: six of nine judged the rate not clearly sufficient to return inflation to target, citing rising inflation pressures, strong services inflation and a likely higher neutral rate, while the three dissenters argued it was prudent to wait and assess the 100 basis points already delivered this year, pointing to delayed effects, higher-than-expected unemployment and the housing downturn. The dissent was about timing, not about the cycle being over, and no explicit guidance was given. That follows Bullock at 00:50 on Monday keeping inflation risks skewed to the upside and flagging high oil. Against it: TradingEconomics has the market implying an 82% probability rates have peaked, CommBank expects a December hold, and the board's own November guidance has inflation reaching the top of the 2 to 3 per cent band only in late 2027 with unemployment rising more than previously anticipated. The Q3 wage price index lands Wednesday 02:30 forecast plus 1.0% on the quarter, and October employment Thursday 02:30 forecast plus 25,500 after minus 39,329.

NZD.when: December 9 at 03:00, a full Monetary Policy Statement, and the forecaster split is still unresolved
NZD.note: The official cash rate is 2.75% after October's hold, taken 4-3 against market pricing that had been near 90% for a hike - a genuine surprise. The committee said tighter policy is likely to be required, depending on the outlook, and flagged near-term inflation uncertainty from volatile oil and fuel prices. Today's Q4 inflation expectations at 04:00 was the direct input and it was close to neutral: the two-year gauge the bank watches most edged to 2.36% from 2.34% on TradingEconomics, while the one-year measure jumped to 2.92% from 2.60% and survey respondents put the cash rate at 3.05% by the end of December, which implies a hike. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% for December 9 and Westpac looks for December and February moves to a 3.5% neutral, while ANZ has pencilled in a pause. Headline CPI is 3.7% and falling, under the bank's own 3.9% forecast, but its published track has inflation worsening to about 4.4% in Q4. Governor Breman spoke at 02:00 and nothing from it is yet verifiable; he speaks again Wednesday 20:00.

CAD.when: December 9 at 16:45, a regular decision with no Monetary Policy Report, and energy has now taken it off the table rather than off the coin flip
CAD.note: The overnight rate is 2.50% after October's quarter-point increase, the first rise in three years. The bank hiked specifically to stop high energy prices spreading into other goods and services, and energy has now fallen about 14% in a month - WTI is 84.87 and down 13.88%, Brent down 16.27%. October CPI did not deliver the acceleration the hike case needed either: m/m plus 0.2% against plus 0.3% forecast, trimmed 1.8% against 1.9%, median 2.0% in line, and headline y/y held at 3.1% where a Reuters poll looked for 3.2%, with core down to 2.0% from 2.2%. The two preferred cores now average 1.9%, below the 2% midpoint, which is not the persistence the bank described in October when it called inflation higher and more persistent than in the July Report and put CPI at an average 3% in 2027. Set against a six-month-high 6.7% jobless rate and a third consecutive monthly employment fall at minus 4,700, a hold is now the clear base case. Gravelle speaks Wednesday 19:30 and retail sales land Friday 15:30, forecast plus 0.7% after plus 1.2%.

CHF.when: December 10 at 10:30, the quarterly assessment, with a hike not expected
CHF.note: The SNB policy rate is 0.00%, unchanged since mid-2025 and held again in September, and previews into December are near-unanimous for another hold. It forecasts average inflation of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in each of 2027 and 2028. October CPI is 1.5%, close to a three-year high, but core is only 0.5%, so the rise is energy - and energy is now falling, which points the next prints lower rather than higher. TradingEconomics also now carries Q3 GDP growth at 0.2% on the quarter, a sharp slowdown from 1.5%, which argues against any tightening impulse. The franc held its modest haven bid for a second session, firmer against the dollar and the euro, which is why it stays at zero rather than going back to minus one. Note the official language has softened, not hardened - the bank removed its prior reference to increased willingness to stem gains in September and officials told lawmakers only that they remain prepared to step in - so December is about the intervention wording rather than the rate.

catalysts.event: Fed Chair Warsh speaks on AI and the economy (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 19:00, a Productivity and Jobs Task Force conference in San Francisco. Opening remarks only, with no rates, no December and no inflation at all. He set out three staff scenarios, labelled illustrative and not forecasts: broadly shared productivity gains; an expansion with substantial labour-market disruption; and a bust where, after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns turn down and the economy slows. Productivity has been reasonably strong but has not yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside, and the Fed's role is neither advocacy nor opposition. Not market-moving, and December pricing has since firmed to 95.7% without him.

catalysts.event: RBA Governor Bullock speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered at 00:50 on Monday on the ASIC Annual Forum State of the Economy panel in Sydney. She kept the board's view that inflation risks are still skewed to the upside and flagged the risk of oil prices remaining high, with no new December guidance reported and no transcript published. The market was unmoved at the time - AUD/USD went on to 0.67318, minus 0.58% - but the minutes six hours later confirmed her lean rather than contradicting it.

catalysts.event: RBA November meeting minutes
catalysts.note: At 02:30, and the hawkish surprise of the overnight session. Six of nine members judged the cash rate at 4.85% was not clearly sufficient to return inflation to target, citing rising inflation pressures, strong services inflation and a likely higher neutral rate. The three dissenters wanted to hold at 4.60%, arguing it was prudent to wait and assess the 100 basis points already delivered this year and pointing to delayed effects of tightening, higher-than-expected unemployment and the housing downturn. No explicit guidance was given. This file had named the dissenters holding on substance as its invalidation; they held on timing, so the Aussie moves from minus two to minus one. CommBank still expects a December hold.

It did not rescue the currency: NZD/USD fell for a sixth straight session to fresh 18-month lows at 0.54947, weakest against all seven others. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% for December 9 while ANZ expects a pause.

catalysts.event: US October retail sales and core retail sales (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 15:30, and it went the hawkish way on both lines. Headline retail sales rose 0.2% against a plus 0.1% forecast after plus 0.8%, and core - retail sales excluding autos - rose 0.6% against plus 0.4% after plus 0.9%. TradingEconomics confirms both actuals and carries September ex-autos revised up to 1.1%, while its own house consensus for the headline was 0.2%, so the genuine surprise sits in core. Both lines still decelerated hard from September, so the consumer beat a bar that had been cut twice rather than accelerating. The market read it as hawkish: DXY went to 103.638 and plus 0.09% from 103.472 and minus 0.11%, through the 19-month high it had stalled under, with EUR/USD, AUD/USD and USD/CHF all flipping and gold giving back a plus 0.50% morning. The three-session failure of the dollar to bid, which this file had named as its crack, closed inside ten minutes. Waller speaks at 16:10 and Hammack at 16:30, with Musalem at 14:30 and Williams at 21:25.

catalysts.event: Nvidia October-quarter results, after the US close
catalysts.note: The biggest event of the week that no red-folder list carries, and the single clearest invalidation of four separate theses here: the yen at plus one, the franc at zero, the silver short and the Aussie short. This is the first quarter after Jensen Huang's exit. Consensus revenue is about 109 billion dollars with adjusted earnings near 2.47 dollars a share, and options price an earnings-day move around 7.8%. The stock is 156.14 and minus 4.12% going in. The reaction lands in Wednesday's Asian and European sessions.

catalysts.event: Australia Q3 wage price index
catalysts.note: At 02:30, forecast plus 1.0% on the quarter after plus 0.8%, with the annual rate last at 3.2%. One of the RBA's stated conditions for inflation persistence, and it matters more after minutes in which six of nine called 4.85% not clearly sufficient. A hot print is the main scheduled thing that could reopen the December 8 hike the market has written off at 82%.

catalysts.event: UK October CPI (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 09:00, forecast 3.6% from 3.5% with core steady at 2.8% and RPI at 4.1%. The week's binary for sterling and the thing that decides whether the only genuinely unpriced December on this board stays live. The MPC hiked to 4.00% on November 5 by 8-1 with Mann dissenting for 50bp and projects CPI rising to around 5% by mid-2027. A print at 3.4% or below makes December 17 much harder and turns GBP/USD into a short.

catalysts.event: BoE Governor Bailey speaks
catalysts.note: At 09:30, half an hour after the CPI print, which makes this the most informative half-hour of the week for sterling. Bailey has said another increase may be needed unless inflation risks ease while warning against reading November as the start of a long series of rises.

catalysts.event: ECB Financial Stability Review, final CPI and Lagarde
catalysts.note: The review at 11:00, euro-area final October CPI at 12:00 forecast to confirm 4.0% with core at 2.5%, and Lagarde at 16:25, the first of her three appearances this week. A revision lower would matter more than usual now that EU gas has turned down 3.58% on the month: the hike is bought with energy, so a falling energy leg undercuts the three further moves the market prices over the next year.

catalysts.event: BoE Governor Bailey speaks again (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 17:00, his second appearance of the day and the one ForexFactory carries as the red folder. A second chance to firm up or walk back whatever the morning's remarks and the CPI print did to December 17 pricing, with Deputy Governor Lombardelli having kept the meeting open without committing.

catalysts.event: BoC's Gravelle and RBNZ's Breman speak
catalysts.note: Gravelle at 19:30 and Breman at 20:00. Gravelle is the first chance for the Bank of Canada to defend its October framing - inflation higher and more persistent than in the July Report, CPI averaging 3% in 2027 - against a CPI miss and crude down 13.88% on the month; anything hawkish puts December 9 back in play. Breman speaks after the inflation expectations print and is one of the four who voted to hold in October.

catalysts.event: FOMC October 28 meeting minutes (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 21:00, and the real Fed event of this week. The October 28 meeting held at 3.75% to 4.00% with Governor Cook and Cleveland's Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point rise. What the market needs is the width of the hawkish bloc behind those two: a wide one supports a path now priced at 95.7% for December with 69.4% on a cumulative fifty by January, a narrow one is the strongest argument yet against the dollar at plus two.

catalysts.event: Australia October employment and unemployment rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: At 02:30, forecast plus 25,500 after September's minus 39,329, with the unemployment rate expected to hold at 4.7%. This is now the live two-way risk on the week's most crowded short, and more so after hawkish minutes took the policy leg of that short away: the Aussie is at minus one rather than minus two, so a strong print bounces AUD/USD hard. A second negative month confirms the RBA's own warning that unemployment rises more than previously anticipated.

catalysts.event: US jobless claims and Philly Fed, plus Lagarde
catalysts.note: Claims forecast 199,000 after 200,000 and the Philadelphia Fed index 19.2 after 20.9, both at 15:30, with Lagarde also speaking at 15:30. Hammack speaks at 15:50, Jefferson at 16:25, Goolsbee at 19:30 and Barkin at 23:00 - a heavy Fed roster the day after the minutes, which is where the hawkish-bloc question gets tested in person.

catalysts.event: Japan October national core CPI
catalysts.note: At 01:30, forecast 2.3% from 2.1%. The last large data input before the December 18 meeting, where TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% and traders are reported as fully priced. Tokyo core CPI already ran 2.2% in November against a 2.1% forecast without moving the pair - the yen is trading the haven bid and Tokyo's intervention warnings now, not the inflation print.

catalysts.event: UK retail sales, Canada retail sales and Lagarde
catalysts.note: UK retail sales at 09:00 forecast 0.0% after minus 0.4%, with public sector net borrowing at 18.0 billion the same hour; Lagarde at 10:15, her third appearance of the week; and Canadian retail sales at 15:30 forecast plus 0.7% after plus 1.2%, the first hard read on the Canadian consumer since the CPI miss. Bundesbank's Nagel also speaks at 15:00.

catalysts.event: Fed's Waller speaks and revised UoM inflation expectations
catalysts.note: Waller at 15:25 and the revised University of Michigan survey at 17:00, with sentiment forecast at 52.1 from 51.0 and inflation expectations last 4.3%. Waller matters this week specifically because he has said a fifty-point move should be considered in December - though the market now prices that December tail at only 4.3% and has moved the hawkishness to January instead. Cook speaks at 19:15.

catalysts.event: RBA cash rate decision
catalysts.note: At 05:30. A hold at 4.85% is still the base case - the market implies an 82% probability rates have peaked and CommBank expects a hold - but the November minutes make it closer than that, with six of nine members judging the current rate not clearly sufficient to return inflation to target. Wednesday's wage price index and Thursday's jobs are what confirm or break it.

catalysts.event: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: At 03:00, a full statement with new forecasts, and now the clearest invalidation of a kiwi at minus one. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% from 2.75% and Westpac looks for December and February moves to a 3.5% neutral, while ANZ expects a pause - an unusually wide split. Today's survey put respondents' end-December OCR at 3.05%, which implies a hike even as the currency makes fresh 18-month lows.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada rate decision
catalysts.note: At 16:45, a regular decision with no Monetary Policy Report. A hold is now the clear base case rather than a coin flip: October CPI missed on two of three lines, the two preferred cores average 1.9%, and crude is down 13.88% on the month against a bank that hiked in October specifically to stop energy spreading into other goods and services.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision and new projections
catalysts.note: At 21:00, with a fresh Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot. CME-based measures price 95.7% for a quarter-point, which would take the range to 4.00% to 4.25%, with only a 4.3% tail for fifty basis points - the hawkishness has moved to January, where cumulative pricing is 69.4% for fifty. The projections are where the second hike the market now expects gets confirmed or capped.

catalysts.event: SNB quarterly monetary policy assessment
catalysts.note: At 10:30. A hold at 0.00% is near-unanimous in previews. Watch instead for the language on FX intervention, which is what actually caps the franc - and note it has softened rather than hardened, with the bank dropping its reference to increased willingness in September. Q3 growth at 0.2% on the quarter from 1.5% and core CPI at 0.5% argue against any tightening impulse.

catalysts.event: Bank of England Bank Rate decision
catalysts.note: At 14:00, and still genuinely two-sided - the only December outside the US that is not effectively priced, which is the whole reason sterling sits above the euro. A hike would take Bank Rate to 4.25% from 4.00%. Today's earnings print, Wednesday's CPI and Bailey's two appearances are what move it.

catalysts.event: ECB rate decision and press conference
catalysts.note: At 15:15, the final meeting of 2026. All 71 economists in the November 10 to 12 Reuters poll expect the deposit rate at 2.75%, but only 46 call it the peak and 25 see another in early 2027 - and the market is more hawkish still, with traders priced for three moves over the next year. New staff projections accompany it, and the energy assumptions matter now that EU gas has turned down 3.58% on the month.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan policy decision
catalysts.note: At 05:00. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% from 1.25%, traders are reported as fully pricing the move and Commerzbank says the soft Q3 GDP does not change its call. Nearly three-quarters of a Reuters panel expect another dissent at the next hike to weigh on the yen, which is the detail that matters more than the decision - and the nearer risk is the Ministry of Finance at 160, not the Bank.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz, Iran and US talks
catalysts.note: The direction has turned decisively and the level has not. US-facilitated transits are averaging about 33.8 vessels a day on UANI's count with a record 135 over November 8 to 11, and the JMIC counted about 28 a day from November 12 to 14 - against a 2025 baseline near 138 a day and an IMF PortWatch count of three transits on November 8 versus a pre-crisis 85. The JMIC still rates the strait severe with deliberate hostile action highly likely and 183 confirmed regional incidents since March 1. Two tankers were reported to have exploded there on Monday and the US struck Iranian missile launchers across southern Iran on Sunday night. Qatari mediators are working a framework trading an end to Iranian attacks for the lifting of the US port blockade, while Iran's security council says the strait stays closed until its seven conditions are met. The downside in crude is now a slide; the upside is still a gap.

geopolitics: The transmission to watch has flipped from a premium that would not bid to a premium that is actively leaving. For weeks this file argued that a risk premium which fails to respond to escalation is a premium being unwound; today that unwinding has a cause and a number. WTI is 84.87 and minus 1.00%, Brent 91.72 and minus 0.78%, and those sit on a 3.2% to 3.5% collapse on Monday that took the monthly moves to minus 13.88% and minus 16.27% - against minus 9.92% for WTI in yesterday's file. The driver is the physical one: transits through the Strait of Hormuz are recovering. United Against Nuclear Iran puts US-facilitated transits at an average 33.8 vessels a day with a record 135 over the November 8 to 11 window, and the Joint Maritime Information Centre counted 83 from November 12 to 14, about 28 a day. The International Energy Agency forecasts a fourth-quarter surplus and Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average 88 dollars in 2027 and ease to 78 by the end of that year. A correction of emphasis is required, though, because some reporting has gone further than the counts support: flows are not back near pre-war levels. The JMIC baseline is about 138 vessels a day for 2025 and the IMF's PortWatch recorded three transits on November 8 against a pre-crisis baseline near 85, so recovering traffic is still a fraction of normal traffic. Nor has the shooting stopped - the JMIC rates the strait severe with deliberate hostile action highly likely and 183 confirmed regional incidents since March 1, two more tankers were reported to have exploded in the strait on Monday, and the United States struck Iranian missile launchers across southern Iran on Sunday night. Diplomacy is indirect rather than dead: Qatari mediators are working a framework in which Iran ends its attacks in exchange for the United States lifting its blockade of Iran's ports, Iran's deputy foreign minister says a two-day plan to reopen the strait remains on the table contingent on US action, and Iran's security council says the strait stays closed until its seven conditions are met. The FX read follows directly and it costs the Canadian dollar two points rather than one. The Bank of Canada hiked in October specifically to stop high energy prices spreading into other goods and services, and energy has fallen about 14% in a month, which removes the mechanism rather than merely weakening it - so CAD goes to minus two, USD/CAD becomes the widest score gap on the board and USOIL flips from a range to a short. But the distribution is still not symmetric, and that is why the short carries low-medium conviction rather than high: LSEG's point stands that even a diplomatic agreement would not quickly restore normal shipments, because mine clearance, insurance costs and shipowners' willingness to sail all lag any deal, and the same logic in reverse means a single escalation can gap what a month of convoys has slowly bled. The European gas leg has turned with crude and it now cuts the other way for the first time in weeks: EU gas is 84.89 euros and minus 3.58% on the month, against plus 2.39% a day ago, still plus 167.84% on the year. That removes the headwind this file has carried against GER40 and, more importantly for FX, undercuts the argument that the ECB's December hike is being bought with energy - headline HICP is 4.0% against core steady at 2.5%, so a falling energy leg weakens the case for the three further moves the market prices over the coming year. On the haven side the ranking is unchanged from yesterday and now has two sessions behind it: the yen first, the franc second, the dollar and gold not at all. USD/JPY is 159.179 and minus 0.18%, USD/CHF 0.83890 and minus 0.11%, DXY 103.472 and minus 0.11% in a third risk-off session, and gold at 3,875.92 is up 0.50% on the day but still minus 6.40% on the month. That is a rates-dominant risk-off in which havens are chosen rather than bought as a group, which is why the franc holds at zero and the metals shorts stay on.
